question: A 65-year-old African-American man presents to your office with dysphagia. He reports that he has found it progressively more difficult to swallow food over the past year. At the time of presentation, he is able to eat only soup. Social history is significant for asbestos exposure, multiple daily drinks of hard alcohol, and a 70 pack-year smoking history. What would you most expect to see on an esophageal biopsy of this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "65-year-old African-American man" -> "progressive dysphagia over the past year" -> "risk factors include asbestos exposure, alcohol use, and smoking" -> "increased risk for esophageal cancer" -> "esophageal biopsy likely shows keratin nests and pearls" -> 85%

CHAIN: "65-year-old man with dysphagia" -> "history of significant smoking and alcohol use" -> "possible development of squamous cell carcinoma" -> "esophageal biopsy reveals keratin nests and pearls" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Patient with progressive dysphagia" -> "high risk for esophageal malignancy due to lifestyle factors" -> "esophageal biopsy expected to show abnormal cellular changes" -> "keratin nests and pearls indicative of squamous cell carcinoma" -> 75%
CHAIN: "Dysphagia in a high-risk patient" -> "consideration of esophageal pathology" -> "biopsy results may show various changes" -> "keratin nests and pearls suggest squamous cell carcinoma" -> 70%
analysis: The patient's history of progressive dysphagia, significant smoking and alcohol use, and asbestos exposure raises suspicion for esophageal cancer, particularly squamous cell carcinoma, which is more common in African-American men. On biopsy, one would expect to see keratin nests and pearls, which are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma. Glandular metaplasia (Barrett's esophagus) is more associated with adenocarcinoma, which is less likely given the patient's risk factors and demographics.
